Latest Update: ‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs.
  • According to recent reports, while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients.
  • And yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her upcoming friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

According to recent reports, while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

And yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

The whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

“In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” mentioned Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”.

According to recent reports, the scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her upcoming companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

Industry observers note that “I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” noted Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”.

Recent findings suggest that hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

It has been revealed that “The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very crucial and really supports this scene,” said Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”.

Sources indicate that one topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he said that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

According to recent reports, “I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” remarked Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”.

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi mentioned no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”.

Sources indicate that “There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

According to recent reports, “For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very important turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”.

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

For instance, Resident Evil 10 will be an enormous milestone for the franchise and could possibly feature the return of S.T.A.R.S. Alpha Team’s Jill Valentine, and which mainline entry is chosen to be remade after Resident Evil Veronica may be quite telling.

According to recent reports, there are Resident Evil remake rumors floating about with regard to virtually every game that hasn’t yet been remade, to be fair, but one could be more intriguing than the rest. Indeed, anyone who is a massive fan of Resident Evil 5 may not want to hold their breath. It could be a long but satisfying road to Capcom finally succumbing and exploring co-op gameplay again, and it may take a highly anticipated detour to a duology that fans are itching to revisit.

According to Dusk Golem, as per Twitter/X, “the possibility of doing a Rev 1 Remake has been tossed around.” Again, there are few Resident Evil games that haven’t had their names thrown around with the rumor or potential for them to one day receive a remake of their own, and it was only a matter of time until a sliver of credence was leant toward the belief that Resident Evil Revelations would be treated to one. Plus, if Resident Evil Revelations gets a remake, it’s almost guaranteed that its sequel will, too.

Fans seem to be generally excited about Resident Evil Revelations possibly receiving a remake, though user AKA_Sparda is skeptical about how bloated Capcom’s release schedule might be thereafter. Moreover, user Vagabond85 argues that they’d be pleased to see a Resident Evil Revelations remake make some tonal changes, writing, “The hypersexualization of characters like Jessica really kill the tone of an otherwise pretty strong entry.” However, remakes of Resident Evil Revelations and Resident Evil Revelations 2 would be thrilling due to where they land canonically and chronologically in the series.

Before Resident Evil Veronica was officially confirmed as a remake of Resident Evil Code: Veronica, it seemed unlikely that we’d ever get one. Resident Evil Code: Veronica is set between Resident Evil 3: Nemesis and Resident Evil 4, for instance, and thus, Resident Evil Veronica is launching out of order. This essentially means that any random Resident Evil game could get a remake and simply be sewn into the fabric of the remake timeline that’s been woven, but a Resident Evil Revelations remake would give much-needed context for the franchise’s most epic rivalry.

Ironically, Resident Evil Revelations is set before Resident Evil 5, after the events of Resident Evil Code: Veronica. And, because Resident Evil’s Chris Redfield appears in Code: Veronica, Revelations, and Resident Evil 5, a remake trilogy dedicated to Chris may be in store. Resident Evil Revelations and Revelations 2 are fairly distinct gameplay-wise, and their stories are incredibly unique with pieces of narrative and lore that are barely even remarked on in other mainline Resident Evil installments, so having them remade and repackaged for a new generation of players would be terrific.

#143013. iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it debuted in 2017.
  • Industry observers note that with iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch.
  • According to recent reports, the setup is simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it debuted in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

Industry observers note that with iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the newly introduced GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 ($149, reg. $249) experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

According to recent reports, the setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Recent findings suggest that once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

Industry observers note that as a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

GymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

AirPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

Apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

It has been revealed that iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods consumers a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

Recent findings suggest that in testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t enhancement as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk highlighted 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

Recent findings suggest that I had been getting the impression that gym equipment manufacturers had been abandoning GymKit support - if they ever had done so initially. I even got the impression that the majority of equipment in Apple's own onsite Gym at the Apple Park may not have supported it - at least originally.

It has been revealed that does Apple have a webpage listing compatible brands and models? Like they do/did for HomeKit.

Recent findings suggest that what is other people perception? Any rowing machines that support it?

…checks - surprisingly it looks like Peloton do support it on their bikes.

Recent findings suggest that if I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

AirPods heart-rate permission also matters. You can manage it in Settings under your AirPods settings and privacy options. I had turned it off, mostly as a theoretical battery-saving move, but this test convinced me to turn it back on. AirPods Pro 3 can also work with Apple Watch to provide the best available heart-rate data.

GymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics.

If you’re an artist and you use social media, you’ve probably heard about Ohuhu by now. This brand swiftly made a name for itself simply because they offered high-quality alcohol based markers at prices that undercut competitors. I have to admit that I turned my nose up at them at first; I didn’t believe they could be as good as the markers I already owned when they cost so much less.

In short, I should have listened to Ohuhu’s supporters. I was able to try out both the Honolulu 2S alcohol markers, and my first ever set of acrylics with the Hilo brush tip acrylic paint markers. I was blown away by both.

Perfect for artists of all skill levels, the Ohuhu Hilo markers come in packs of 48 or 72 and are an affordable option compared to rivals. They have a soft brush tip and can be layered up on the page for an opaque finish.

Ohuhu's Honolulu 2S alcohol markers come in a huge range of colors, with 320 markers in the biggest set! These dual-ended markers feature a brush and a chisel tip. While you'll need to watch out for bleed through, they produce a beautiful and smooth finish.

According to recent reports, I started off with the Hilo acrylic markers. These markers have a single, soft and flexible brush tip, and you can currently get either a set of 48 or a set of 72 at Amazon. I was excited to see how they would perform, so I stuck a Holiday movie on, sat back and got out a coloring book to test them out.

Sources indicate that as soon as the pen touched the page, I was immediately struck by the vibrancy of the colors and the opacity of the ink. Sure, the first sections of color I filled in were the blacks, but I couldn’t believe my eyes when the numbers almost disappeared under the acrylic ink. Some of the colors are less effective at this than others — but layer the ink up a few times, and you’ll have one gorgeously clean looking coloring page!

It has been revealed that as for the experience of using them, the soft tips give plenty of control. They felt incredibly smooth to use across gentle curves and coloring medium to large areas was easy and comfortable. These acrylic markers give you the ability to go over and redo areas you’re not happy with if you accidentally color over something you didn’t want to, which is a huge bonus.

According to recent reports, another positive under this set’s belt is the carrying case.The design is so cheerful that it immediately put a smile on my face the first time I saw it, and it honestly still does every time I open it. And compared to other name brand acrylic markers, they’re significantly cheaper — the 72 set works out to around 70 cents per marker at the Black Friday sale price.

According to recent reports, there are some downsides to contend with. When it came to coloring small, detailed areas... I pretty much had to forget about staying within the lines. I struggled to achieve fine pointed shapes and found that the ink pooled into circular shapes every time I attempted them. I also had concerns with streaky ink, and my coloring paper pilled in certain spots, too.

It has been revealed that this is my first time using acrylic markers, so I’m willing to acknowledge all these problems could come down to my lack of skills. I’m going to keep using them and see if I can improve my technique and layer up more to combat the streaks. The pilling probably isn’t going away until I get a coloring book with higher quality paper, though.

Next up, I tried the Honolulu 2S alcohol based markers. You get more color options here as the sets come in packs of 24 all the way up to 320; and these markers have a dual tip. One side has a brush tip, and the other is a chisel tip.

According to recent reports, compared to the Hilo's, the Honolulu 2S’s brush tip is firmer and stiffer. Even though the Hilo brush tip felt great, I liked the Honolulu 2S’s firmer brush tip even more, and found it easier to control when coloring detailed areas and sharp points. It still handles curves just as well, and the chisel tip comes in handy for filling large areas too. I fell in love with alcohol-based markers years back because they produce a beautiful, non-streaky finish. The Honolulu 2S markers absolutely live up to that and looked fantastic on the page.

However, using alcohol based inks comes with more of a learning curve. I started off filling in a large black area on the page once again, and was very impressed that the marker didn’t bleed much at all. However, other colors like the dark blue and gray didn’t fare so well, and bled right over the lines.

Recent findings suggest that the bleed can be mitigated by using paper made specifically for alcohol markers, but you don’t have that option if you want to color in a specific coloring book. It took an hour or two for me to get used to it, but I eventually learned to leave plenty of space while filling areas in to account for the bleed.

It has been revealed that as well as bleeding over the lines, I also had to watch out for the ink bleeding through the paper — Ohuhu provides a plastic sheet to place under your work to avoid staining the next page in your sketchbook. The ink in the Honolulu 2S markers was clearly visible on the back side of the paper I colored on (seen on the left of the image below,) but none got through to the next page. Meanwhile, the back side of the page I colored with the Hilo markers (seen on the right below) was completely clean.

According to recent reports, if you’re a budding artist, I highly recommend picking up a set of Ohuhu markers. The Hilo acrylic markers are the ones for you if you want the most vibrancy, and are also great if you want to have the option to redo areas if you’re not happy with them. Meanwhile, the Honolulu 2S markers stand out for their enormous color selection, excellent brush tip and super-smooth finish.

According to recent reports, these markers are cheaper than the big brands, and are even better value when discounted. Grab them while you can!

#143011. Industry News: 5 Best Book Series To Read If You Like The Hunger Games

Industry News: 5 Best Book Series To Read If You Like The Hunger Games

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, unless you've been living under a rock for multiple decades, you've probably heard of "The Hunger Games." Written by Suzanne Collins, this hybrid of "Battle Royale" and reality television hit shelves in 2008 and introduced readers around the world to Katniss Everdeen, a young woman trying to support her family with illegal game hunting in the deeply impoverished District 12 of a reformed North America known as Panem.
  • In a recent development, "The Hunger Games" kicked off the property of the same name and was followed by sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay," released in 2009 and 2010.
  • It has been revealed that if you've already read all of the "Hunger Games" books and seen all the movies (including the pretty great movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," which is now out in theaters), what should you check out next?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, unless you've been living under a rock for multiple decades, you've probably heard of "The Hunger Games." Written by Suzanne Collins, this hybrid of "Battle Royale" and reality television hit shelves in 2008 and introduced readers around the world to Katniss Everdeen, a young woman trying to support her family with illegal game hunting in the deeply impoverished District 12 of a reformed North America known as Panem. When Katniss' beloved younger sister Primrose is chosen, or "reaped," via a random lottery to participate in the annual Games (where two "tributes" from all 12 districts are forced to compete to the death on live television until one victor emerges), Katniss volunteers as tribute, and her time as a Hunger Games participant begins.

In a recent development, "The Hunger Games" kicked off the property of the same name and was followed by sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay," released in 2009 and 2010. Naturally, a "Hunger Games" film franchise followed in 2012 and spawned four blockbusters. ("Mockingjay" got split into two parts, something that director Francis Lawrence regrets.) Then, in 2020, Collins released her first literary "Hunger Games" prequel, "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" — which centers on the origin story of future Panem president Coriolanus Snow — and five years later, we got "Sunrise on the Reaping," which explains precisely how Katniss' eventual friend and mentor (and her fellow District 12 victor) Haymitch Abernathy won his Games.

It has been revealed that if you've already read all of the "Hunger Games" books and seen all the movies (including the pretty great movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," which is now out in theaters), what should you check out next? From dystopian classics to other YA favorites, we've got some ideas.

In a recent development, A lot of dystopian novels are referred to as "speculative fiction," which means that the scenario laid out by the author could conceivably happen in real life ... so, let's hope that Nana Kwame Adjei-Brenyah's novel "Chain-Gang All-Stars" doesn't come to pass. Released in 2023, this novel imagines a world where the incarceration system in the United States is, somehow, even worse than it is in our reality — in that prisoners are allowed to enroll in a program called CAPE, which stands for "Criminal Action Penal Entertainment." Not only are the inmates in CAPE constantly monitored (with their every move broadcast to hungry audiences), they're also sent across the country to constantly participate in gladiator matches against each other that are, you guessed it, televised as well. The book's title comes from the reimagined version of a traditional "chain gang," where the prisoner-gladiators are called "Links" and given two options to leave: either they're High Freed, meaning released, or Low Freed, meaning killed.

In a recent development, throughout "Chain-Gang All-Stars," we follow the Angola-Hammond Chain in the system and, more specifically, Hamara "Hurricane Staxxx" Stacker and Loretta "Blood Mama" Thurwar, the two female fighters in a secret relationship who open the book. As we move through the unsettling world Adjei-Brenyah concocted in "Chain-Gang All Stars," we follow a wide variety of prisoners participating in this gut-wrenching game ... and it's sort of impossible to not think of the "Hunger Games" franchise as you read it, albeit in a good way. After you wrap up all five "Hunger Games" books, check out "Chain-Gang All-Stars." (Nina Starner).

In a recent development, when it comes to seeing people die horrible deaths in death games televised for the entertainment of an oppressive ruling class, no book does it on a larger scale than Matt Dinniman's "Dungeon Crawler Carl." The book takes place after Earth has been taken over by an alien corporation that seeks to mine the planet for resources. Those who aren't killed during the initial invasion are then forced to compete in an intergalactic reality show program, an RPG-like "dungeon crawl" where they have to navigate various levels of a labyrinthian dungeon, each filled with increasingly dangerous monsters and scenarios.

What makes "Dungeon Crawler Carl" unique is how it blends together ridiculous video game and tabletop RPG logic with an unhealthy dose of pop culture references, the humor of a Douglas Adams book, and the brutality and social commentary about unchecked capitalism and authoritarianism of "The Hunger Games." Indeed, reading Dinniman's book and its follow-ups is like playing a fun RPG session, in that it's chaotic, messy, hilarious, and weird, all while packing a serious emotional punch full of heartbreak and cruel twists and turns. But rather than reveling in their misery, Dinniman's characters rage against the corporate machine in an effort to break it. What you end up with is a story about the necessity of resistance and the importance of community, both of which are themes that will resonate with "Hunger Games" fans. And did I mention it features an endlessly quotable talking cat? (Rafael Motamayor).

In a recent development, I don't think it's possible to have a conversation about young adult dystopian books and films like the "Hunger Games" stories without discussing "The Handmaid's Tale." Margaret Atwood's landmark 1980 book set a standard for dystopian narratives rivaled only by George Orwell's "1984," but Atwood's specificity is what makes her imagined world so terrifying — in that "The Handmaid's Tale" takes place in a world where a religious totalitarian regime oppresses women and queer people. Offred (meaning "of Fred"), our heroine, works as one of the titular handmaids, which means she's prized for her fertility and used as a "vessel" (that's putting it politely) for her Commander, Fred, to impregnate instead of his un-fertile wife. As Offred exists in Gilead (which forbids women from having quite literally any rights and punishes them with death if they even try to stray), we follow her every move in the novel, learning bits and pieces about her life before Gilead as June, a mother and wife with the freedom to live as she pleased.

Sources indicate that "The Handmaid's Tale" was adapted into a Hulu series in 2017, and while I do think Elisabeth Moss did an incredible job playing Offred, the show ran through Atwood's book by the end of Season 1 and kept its wheels spinning for, in my opinion, far too long (although it at least gets its final message right.) If you haven't read Atwood's book but are familiar with its well-known red costumes and overall vibe, I couldn't possibly recommend it more. Its prose is beautiful, its subject matter is terrifying, and it's a clear precursor to and inspiration for the stories found in the "Hunger Games" franchise. (Nina Starner).

Though certainly not as dark in tone as "The Hunger Games," the pop culture celebration that is author Ernest Cline's "Ready Player One" is an oddly fitting companion piece for fans of the world Suzanne Collins built. One could even look at it as a bit of a palette cleanser, albeit one that still scratches a similar itch.

For those not familiar, the book takes place in 2044 and focuses on Wade Watts, who spends his days in the virtual utopia known as the OASIS. Wade's devoted his life to studying the puzzles hidden within this world's digital confines, themselves based on their creator's fixation on pop culture — with the promise of massive power and fortune to whoever can unlock them.

"Ready Player One" is jam-packed with pop culture references and is lighthearted in a lot of ways. However, it's also terribly dystopian, as the OASIS is not only people's sole escape from the harsh realities of the outside world, there's very little person-to-person communication anymore outside of the virtual space. Beyond that, the rush to solve the puzzles and nab the fortune results in a deadly game for Wade and many others, which is where the "Hunger Games" of it all comes in.

It has been revealed that steven Spielberg's 2018 movie adaptation left a lot to be desired for many fans and, yes, a "Ready Player Two" movie was in the works in 2021, though it's yet to materialize. Setting the film aside, the novel remains a true gem filled with wonderful world building, fully-realized characters, and just a dash of "kill or be killed" to make the whole thing extra exciting, elevating it beyond the barrage of references it might have otherwise been. (Ryan Scott).

According to recent reports, the funny thing about Pierce Brown's "Red Rising" series is that the first book in the still-ongoing saga is very much a "Hunger Games" riff ... until it's not. Set in a distant future where humanity has been rigidly split into various genetically modified castes that determine a person's role in society, the story follows Darrow, a young Martian "red" whose wife is murdered by the ruling "gold" regime, sending him on a quest for revenge that ultimately spans the entire solar system. But before the sweeping space opera can begin, Darrow infiltrates the gold caste and must survive the Institute, a deadly school where young people are violently set against one another in not-so-simulated combat and conquest.

Those who enjoyed the blend of youthful angst, action, sci-fi world-building, and dystopian politics of "The Hunger Games" will take rapidly and easily to "Red Rising," which offers a similar flavor with a harsher, more masculine edge. However, starting with the second book "Golden Son" and continuing into later installments, Brown takes things in a wholly fresh direction, turning his Suzanne Collins riff into the kind of sprawling, detailed, intense, and morally murky epic that would make Frank Herbert and George R.R. Martin proud. This is the perfect stepping stone for "Hunger Games" fans hoping to branch out into a different flavor of science fiction. It's familiar enough, until it is suddenly, and brutally, not. (Jacob Hall).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The Hawk,” a Will Ferrell golf comedy that debuted just this summer, has been canceled by Netflix and will not return for a second season, an individual with knowledge told IndieWire.

Ferrell co-created the series in which he plays a former top golfer who is now trying to return to the tour. And while it figured to be a tentpole series for Netflix, one that carried possibly the most expensive budget for a comedy series on Netflix and reunited Ferrell with his “SNL” co-star Molly Shannon and co-creator Harper Steele, it didn’t connect with critics or audiences.

“The Hawk” spent just three weeks on Netflix’s Top 10 when it debuted back in July, topping out at #2 in its second week on Netflix with just 6.2 million views. Ferrell’s vulgar, loudly-dressed golfer with a personalized visor and substantial mess of bleached blonde hair played a lot like some of Ferrell’s other string of sports comedies throughout the years. But even our critic was perplexed by the series’ tone that makes it sometimes play like a “bizarre addiction drama.” Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down.

Steele, in a recent appearance on “Late Night with Seth Meyers,” tipped her hand a little that the show was likely ending when she let slip that, “I was working on a short-lived but probably the best show ever, ‘The Hawk.’”.

In a recent development, the cancellation comes in the wake of a changing of the guard at Netflix, with Peter Rice taking over for veteran creative chief Bela Bajaria. Our critic also recently wrote about the challenges Netflix is facing right now in getting audiences to discover latest series in the ways they used to.

But at the same time, Netflix has already renewed a couple of other comedy series that even premiered after “The Hawk” later this year, including “Nobody Wants This,” “A Different World,” “Tires,” “Major Mistakes,” and “The Four Seasons.” Netflix is also still working with Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions on three fresh series, “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and another scripted series from Nikki Glaser.

Deadline first reported the news.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"The Hunger Games" franchise is back with a story fans have been waiting a very long time for. "Sunrise on the Reaping" is the darkest movie in "The Hunger Games" series, flashing back to the famed games in which Haymitch Abernathy won. Originally played by Woody Harrelson, that character is a fan-favorite, but this movie does a lot of work to help fill in crucial elements of his character, played this time by Joseph Zada.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place on the "Hunger Games" timeline 24 years before the events of the first movie. It follows sixteen-year-old Haymitch from District 12, beginning on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Annual Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, the biggest Games yet with twice as many tributes. But Haymitch isn't the only classic character who gets more time to shine in this entry.

Recent findings suggest that plenty of "Hunger Games" characters return in this prequel in younger form, including Caesar Flickerman (played by Oscar winner Kieran Culkin) and Effie Trinket (played by Emmy nominee Elle Fanning). But they're not the only ones who will be familiar to fans of the series. There's also the matter of Mags Flanagan, a very crucial character in the history of both the books and the movies. Originally played by Lynn Cohen in "Catching Fire," she won the 11th Hunger Games and volunteered as tribute during the 75th games.

Sources indicate that this time around, the younger version of Cohen is played by actress Lili Taylor. The role is crucial, as Mags is the one who mentors Haymitch en route to his time in the games. But for those who feel Taylor looks familiar, there's a good reason for that: She's a great actress with one heck of a resume.

Lili Taylor got her start as an actress in the late '80s/early '90s, starring in movies such as "Mystic Pizza," "Say Anything," and "Born on the Fourth of July." She worked steadily throughout the '90s in movies, in addition to doing some television, including an episode of "The X-Files." Some of her other notable credits from this period include "Ransom" and "The Haunting.".

Recent findings suggest that one of her earliest, substantial breakout roles came in the early 2000s on "Six Feet Under," one of the best HBO highlights of all time, as Lisa Kimmel. She also continued to work very steadily in movies during this period, earning credits in "Brooklyn's Finest" and "Public Enemies," among others. Though not often in the spotlight as a lead, Taylor tends to use her talents in memorable supporting roles.

The 2010s were particularly kind to Taylor. 2013's "The Conjuring" kicked off the biggest non-Marvel cinematic universe, and she had a major part to play as Carolyn Perron, one of the heads of the household at the center of that movie's haunting. It's arguably her most notable role to date. She reprised the role in "The Nun" and "The Conjuring: Last Rites." That same year, she also starred in "Hemlock Grove," one of the first original highlights produced by Netflix.

Taylor has over 100 credits to her name so we can't possibly go over all of them, but some other titles viewers might recognize her from include "The Maze Runner: The Scorch Trials," "Leatherface," HBO's "Perry Mason," "Outer Range," "Fear Street: Prom Queen," and most recently Marvel's "Daredevil: Born Again," where she played Marge McCaffrey.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that decades after Gary Larson concluded his comic strip The Far Side back in 1995, fans of the series continue to read it regularly, and new fans are discovering it all the time.
  • Larson didn’t just do this with animals, however.
  • Recent findings suggest that here are the eight funniest Far Side comics featuring fruits and vegetables.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that decades after Gary Larson concluded his comic strip The Far Side back in 1995, fans of the series continue to read it regularly, and new fans are discovering it all the time. Some of Larson’s most beloved comic strips feature animals drawn in his signature style, including dogs, chickens, and especially cows. He often gave these animals human-like intelligence and other anthropomorphic traits and depicted them in very human-like scenarios.

Larson didn’t just do this with animals, however. The man had a strong surrealist streak​​​​​​​, and sometimes he’d make all sorts of things the subjects of his comic strips​​​​​​​. This includes fruits and vegetables, which he often paired with a bit of wordplay or some common association with the given food group.

Recent findings suggest that here are the eight funniest Far Side comics featuring fruits and vegetables. You’re also welcome to snack while enjoying them.

Larson began publishing The Far Side on Jan. 1, 1980, making this one of his earliest comics, when it appeared only in The San Francisco Chronicle​​​​​​​. It depicts a frustrated carrot threatening his kids with a terrifying story of how actual carrots are treated.

One of Larson’s signature moves in The Far Side was to take a well-known idiom and interpret it in the most literal way possible. Here, the biblical phrase “forbidden fruit” gets twisted into a comic where a lime is trying to enter a fruit-themed nightclub which doesn’t allow anyone who’s green.

Sources indicate that on second thought, I’m not quite sure if that’s a lime, as it only vaguely resembles one. I don’t recall ever seeing a lime with a stem like that. Perhaps it’s a guava? Or a green plum? I’d say maybe a pear, but it isn’t at all pear-shaped. Perhaps the fruit is some other kind of fruit that isn’t yet ripe​​​​​​​, which means it could be a whole bunch of things. And maybe that’s part of the joke, as he’s not yet ripe enough for the adult nightclub? I’m really not sure.

I’m also unsure whether the fruits in this comic are​​​​​​​ anthropomorphic fruit or if they are people dressed like fruit. Just look at the human-like arms of the banana. That, to me, suggests that the banana is a man in a banana suit, yet his face is more fruit-like.

Mr. Larson, I have a lot of questions about this comic. Please write me at your earliest convenience.

Carrots seem to be a particular favorite of Larson’s as they show up more often than any other vegetable​​​​​​​ (except maybe potatoes). Here, two “Carrots of the evening” try to pick up a passing celery​​​​​​​ as a customer. While we don’t know whether he accepts the offer​​​​​​​, I’m thinking he does and there’s nothing wrong with that. Prostitution should be legal and I don’t see a ring on that celery’s finger.

Mr. Potato Head appeared in a handful of Gary Larson comics​​​​​​​, but this darkly funny one is easily the best. It depicts Mrs. Potato Head on a witness stand, testifying against her husband who had chased her around with a “Veg-o-matic.” I especially love how furious Mr. Potato Head looks here. Even Don Rickles’ Mr. Potato Head from the Toy Story films never had eyes quite this angry.

Nowadays, for the most part, vegetarians are fairly common, but in the 1980s and 1990s, when Gary Larson was still doing The Far Side, it was far less “normal.” As a result, vegetarians became punchlines​​​​​​​ in a number of Larson's comic strips. This one is a great example, in which​​​​​​​ a bunch of “Early vegetarian” cave people triumphantly carry back a carrot. I especially love the detail of them carrying shovels as their weapons.

And here’s a pretty similar comic, but it's worthy of greatness for its depiction of a hairy “Wooly Watermelon.”.

According to recent reports, vegetarians are once again the punchline in Gary Larson’s funniest-ever comic starring fruits and vegetables, as a meat truck is about to crash into Noreen’s Vegetarian Cafe. The horrified faces of Noreen’s patrons make​​​​​​​ this laugh-out-loud funny​​​​​​​.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some sci-fi stories are so profoundly human, introspective, and existential on the page that adapting them on the screen seems impossible.
  • Perhaps Denis Villeneuve’s Arrival is an incredible example of this.
  • It has been revealed that like Denis Villeneuve’s Arrival, Pantheon seems fairly simple in its early moments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some sci-fi stories are so profoundly human, introspective, and existential on the page that adapting them on the screen seems impossible. Even some of the most ambitious filmmakers leave such stories alone. However, every once in a while, someone dares to translate such stories to the screen and the result turns out to be beyond impressive.

Perhaps Denis Villeneuve’s Arrival is an incredible example of this. The sci-fi movie turns Ted Chiang's stories into a masterful exploration of time, destiny, free will, and the stories we tell ourselves to find meaning. Similar to Arrival, the sci-fi series, Pantheon, goes to extreme lengths to capture the essence of Ken Liu's award-winning sci-fi stories.

It has been revealed that like Denis Villeneuve’s Arrival, Pantheon seems fairly simple in its early moments. The sci-fi show on Netflix unfolds in a world where mind-uploading technology is becoming accessible for the masses. However, what starts as a tale about a global conspiracy evolves to an existential scale that questions everything from humanity's place in the universe to the nature of consciousness.

Recent findings suggest that ted Chiang's novella, Story of Your Life, was seemingly never meant to be adapted for the screen. It heavily relies on teleological physics and linguistic relativity to explore time travel. Yet, screenwriter Eric Heisserer and director Denis Villeneuve turned it into a 2-hour cinematic masterpiece by tricking viewers into reading flash-forwards as flashbacks.

Sources indicate that in Pantheon, creator Craig Silverstein picks up many of Ken Liu's short stories that present fragmented explorations of post-humanity. He then binds them into a singular narrative that starts a relatable family drama but grows into an existential war story. Pantheon does not shy away from being incredibly ambitious with its storytelling. But, like Denis Villeneuve's Arrival, it never forgets it is about its human characters.

On the screen, science fiction can risk feeling too sterile and hollow if its ambition outgrows its human stakes. There are cosmic elements in both Arrival and Pantheon that give a glimpse of how insignificant human lives can seem in the vastness of the universe. Yet, in both, the high-concept sci-fi is always anchored in human grief.

Pantheon originally premiered on AMC+, but it is now available for streaming on Netflix in the U.S.

Arrival introduces an alien language through ink-ring logograms to make sense out of an abstract concept like non-linear time. It never dumbs this down and respects viewers' intelligence by allowing them to do a lot of intellectual heavy lifting. Pantheon achieves something similar by using animating as a visual language as it walks through complex ideas surrounding.

In the best existential sci-fi books, post-humanity is the threshold. They question whether a machine can think or whether achieving singularity would be a boon or bane for humanity. Pantheon, in contrast, blows right past this. Boom! The series keeps pushing the boundaries of existential sci-fi until it is far beyond base realities, linear time, and biological life.

It begins with a familiar exploration of how digital cloning and consciousness uploading can pave the way for many moral and ethical challenges. Once uploading becomes safe, it shifts to a civilizational schism, showing how those who refuse to "upload" themselves are biological relics while the ones who conformed are almost godlike.

Industry observers note that before its credits start rolling, Pantheon also ambitiously leaps millions of years ahead in time. With this, it attempts to highlight how, despite becoming almost godly omnipresent beings with the ability to simulate infinity, meaning only exists in human vulnerability and the inability to know what lies ahead. Here lies the beauty of Pantheon's unforgettable exploration of existential sci-fi.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that it's been a funny season, and it's been a heartfelt season at times, particularly when the show killed Kenny (again) and decided to replace him with none other than a kid version of Randy (complete with mustache).
  • In the finale, "City Endings," the town of South Park (renamed this season as South America) is hit with major power outages that disrupt the town's "GTA VI" gametime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that "South Park" has been on a roll recently. When the show finally left behind its Mr.-Garrison-as-Trump allegory and stopped doing endless specials (even if most of those were fantastic), it found its stride again in Season 28, which took on AI and deepfakes in the funniest way possible. Then, Season 29 took on everything from the data centers, to "looksmaxxing" and "aura farming" in a hilarious "Backrooms" parody, to club sports in a great "Heated Rivalry" parody, to the US beef shortage, and more.

Recent findings suggest that it's been a funny season, and it's been a heartfelt season at times, particularly when the show killed Kenny (again) and decided to replace him with none other than a kid version of Randy (complete with mustache). It has even been a romantic season, with the Tweek and Craig romance-focused episode. What "South Park" usually isn't, however, is scary. That changed with the Season 29 finale, which delivered the scariest TV scene of 2026 — twice.

In the finale, "City Endings," the town of South Park (renamed this season as South America) is hit with major power outages that disrupt the town's "GTA VI" gametime. It is part of a conspiracy involving secret deals the government made with billionaire weenies. At the same time, there's paranoia involving supposed Chinese spies and possible cyberattacks from that country.

Sources indicate that in the middle of all this, Cartman, Stan, and Kyle are also haunted by visions of the late Kenny, who died after being blown up by an e-bike in the season's premiere. Except this is not just Kenny, but a zombified version that haunts the boys in the form of horrific ghouls that even infiltrate "GTA VI," like a spectre out of "The Ring.".

"South Park" has toyed with the horror genre before, usually body horror. There was the Michael Jackson parody with Mr. Jefferson slowly rotting away, for example, or the HumanCentipad. The Season 29 finale, however, features one of the wildest and most gruesome eldritch abominations in the nearly 30-year history of the show. It starts with several scenes of Kenny simply standing creepily in the background, stalking the boys as if to try and send a message.

Sources indicate that "City Endings" is a legit horror episode, which is rare from the show that spent nearly a decade on a silly weed farm storyline. The image of Kenny just standing in the background, his face obscured by his hoodie but with bright eyes just shining like Pennywise in "It," is already quite disturbing and terrifying. Then, when the boys finally catch up to Kenny, who leads them to the cemetery and to his own grave, he shows off his gruesome zombie face and starts dissolving like that guy in "Poltergeist," in excruciatingly disturbing detail, before exploding in a pool of blood.

Sources indicate that it's enough to make your skin crawl, but it's not even the scariest scene of the episode. That climax comes in later, while the boys are playing "GTA VI" at Butters' house. We see the zombie Kenny monster with long spiky teeth, deranged eyes and elongated limbs with claws crawling out of the TV like Samara Morgan from "The Ring." It is the stuff of pure nightmares, and by far the scariest scene in 2026 television.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

In a recent development, earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

Sources indicate that at the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

Recent findings suggest that in Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, Latest Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”.

In a recent development, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

Industry observers note that and for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

In a recent development, there are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

According to recent reports, whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, now, Chris Evans has claimed that Doom wears his mask for the entirety of "Doomsday." But that could only mean he'll keep the mask on until "Secret Wars." Even then, there's the chance that Doom is so disfigured that his face isn't even recognizable as RDJ.
  • Sources indicate that in this TV spot, Magneto (Ian McKellen) tries to telekinetically rip off Doom's mask — it is made of metal, after all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that marvel Comics fans know Doctor Victor von Doom is scarcely ever seen without his iron mask — a mask that hides his supposedly horribly scarred face. But with Marvel Studios choosing former Tony Stark actor Robert Downey Jr. to play Doom in the upcoming "Avengers" movies "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars," there's been an expectation that Doom's mask coming off will be a jaw dropping moment.

In a recent development, now, Chris Evans has claimed that Doom wears his mask for the entirety of "Doomsday." But that could only mean he'll keep the mask on until "Secret Wars." Even then, there's the chance that Doom is so disfigured that his face isn't even recognizable as RDJ. A newly introduced TV spot for "Doomsday" does suggest Doom has his scarred face, while also teasing we're eventually going to see exactly what's under his mask ... but not yet.

Sources indicate that in this TV spot, Magneto (Ian McKellen) tries to telekinetically rip off Doom's mask — it is made of metal, after all. But Doom does not restrict himself to the laws of science. There's evidently a magical seal on the mask (note there appear to be runic designs across Doom's costume), because glowing green tendrils extend out from Doom's hood and grab the mask, slamming it back onto Doom's face. A brief glimpse of Doom's face, visible through the mask's eyeholes, reveals hints of pale macerated skin and scar tissue.

Industry observers note that in the "Fantastic Four" comics, it was originally said that Doom suffered his scars during an experiment in college. A machine he built to contact the "nether world" (later revealed to be an attempt to reach his mother's damned soul) exploded in his face, leaving him scarred.

It has been revealed that now, Doom's co-creator Jack Kirby intended that Doom actually only had a thin facial scar — but Doom's ego can't stand even that small imperfection. Later "Fantastic Four" writer/artist John Byrne melded the two ideas. The machine explosion only slightly damaged Doom's face, but then Victor — convinced his face was already ruined — put his freshly forged mask on before it cooled, and that is why he has a horribly scarred face.

The greatest source of Doom's torment is completely self-inflicted. The exemplary 1989 "Doctor Strange and Doctor Doom: Triumph and Torment" goes with Byrne's interpretation. When Doom seeks out the wisdom of the wizard named the Aged Genghis, the sorcerer alludes to Doom's "minor disfigurement." We then see Doom's (barely scarred) face as Victor lashes out at the insult.

It's unclear what origin "Doomsday" will go with, if any of them. Marketing suggests the Marvel Cinematic Universe's Doom will be driven by a lost wife and child, not his mother. What is clear from this TV spot is that Marvel fans can expect to see Doom and Magneto — the two greatest villains of Marvel Comics — clash onscreen. Doom's wizardry here refutes the obvious conclusion that Magneto wins easily because he controls metal and Doom is concealed inside metal armor.

"He is pain, he is extinction," Magneto declares, setting up Doom's famous third person double entendre: "I am Doom!" Ian McKellen's Magneto was the first villain of the Marvel movie boom that kicked off with 2000's "X-Men." Bringing him back to face (and presumably fall to) Doom is some classic carnival barker marketing that would make Stan Lee proud.

"Avengers: Doomsday" is set for theatrical release on December 18, 2026.

8 Essential Thriller Books Everyone Should Read at Least Once

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The safest way to chase an adrenaline rush is to read a captivating thriller book.
  • In a recent development, take genre staples like Gone Girl or The Silent Patient.
  • It has been revealed that the Oscar-winning Conclave was a surprising front-runner in a year dominated by flashier films like Anora and The Brutalist, and its source material is just as disarmingly good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The safest way to chase an adrenaline rush is to read a captivating thriller book. These stories rely on one or more mysteries to ramp up tension, provoke intellectual curiosity, and deliver a sense of catharsis. Fiction is often a safe space to explore uncomfortable emotions, and thrillers deliver on this front by allowing readers to escape into worlds brimming with danger.

In a recent development, take genre staples like Gone Girl or The Silent Patient. While the two couldn’t be more different in tone and subject matter, both thrillers heavily rely on misdirection and the recontextualization of events to deliver twists. These picks are a staple in every “must-read” list for good reason, just like the ones Polygon has highlighted below as genre essentials. Without further ado, here are eight thriller books you should read at least once in your life.

It has been revealed that the Oscar-winning Conclave was a surprising front-runner in a year dominated by flashier films like Anora and The Brutalist, and its source material is just as disarmingly good. The premise of a papal conclave held right after the pope’s death might feel a bit too somber, but Conclave unfolds like a tense political thriller that balances breakneck pacing with intricate detail. Jacopo Lomeli is tasked with the responsibility of overseeing the papal conclave in the event of the tragedy, and four cardinals are promptly chosen as leading candidates. But there’s more to the conspiracy than one would expect, turning the novel into a thrilling clash of ideologies that is also a deft exploration of inner conflict.

The Talented Mr. Ripley introduces us to Tom Ripley, famously played by Matt Damon in Anthony Minghella’s 1999 film adaptation and Andrew Scott in Netflix’s Ripley. Tom is struggling to make ends meet in New York, prompting him to carry out petty cons. When shipping magnate Herbert Greenleaf approaches Ripley to persuade his son, Dickie, to join the family business, the opportunistic young man readily agrees. Patricia Highsmith presents an unforgettable anti-hero, whose actions follow irrefutable internal logic despite being morally wrong. The novel is a fascinating character study about sociable forms of evil and how they manifest when you least expect it.

A “whodunnit” framework propels most mystery thrillers, but The Secret History operates with a tense, slow-burn “why-done-it” narrative. The novel’s unreliable narrator, Richard Papen, immediately tells us about a murder, a crime for which he is “partly responsible.” This curiosity to understand the why and how makes this dark academia campus novel especially riveting. The novel’s secluded setting in Vermont adds to the isolation of the six tight-knit students at its center, whose obsession with all things Ancient Greece comes with a heavy price. Tartt’s characters are flawed, obnoxious, and compelling, successfully retaining our avid interest despite being deliberately disengaged from the world at large.

Blake Crouch has written engaging sci-fi books like Recursion and Upgrade, and Dark Matter leans heavily into sci-fi thriller territory with its propulsive pacing. The story follows physicist Jason Dessen, who is kidnapped and sent to a parallel universe, where his life plays out differently due to a drastically different choice he made in this timeline. In fact, this version of Jason has built a cube that enables travel between countless alternate worlds, which changes his understanding of quantum mechanics. Dark Matter is easily accessible for anyone, as its convoluted premise unfolds in a way that’s fun and easily digestible. This is undoubtedly popcorn entertainment, meant to be read while you’re waiting at the airport.

David Cronenberg’s adaptation of The Dead Zone is both a taut thriller and a quietly melancholic movie about a man with a strange gift. A child named Johnny Smith challenges a prophetic warning after an ice-skating accident, and grows up to become a small-town high school teacher. Things take a turn after an accident-induced coma makes Johnny gain frighteningly accurate psychic abilities, along with a vision of the end of the world. Stephen King’s source material excels in conveying the eerie, lived-in horror of weighing extreme choices to determine the fate of those around us. Johnny’s predicament, although fantastical, feels deeply human in the way the personal and the political seamlessly blend together.

Sources indicate that A bona fide bestseller that has been adapted countless times on the screen, Rebecca is the definition of a Gothic novel with exceptional thriller elements. The book opens with an unnamed narrator lamenting that she cannot return to her husband’s estate, as it has been destroyed. Looking back, she recounts how she married the older, wealthy Maximilian de Winter, whose first wife, Rebecca, drowned in a sailing accident. Although the narrator does her best to acclimatize to her new life, every person at the estate seems haunted by Rebecca’s memory, to the point of undermining the new bride’s sense of self. Rebecca is a timeless classic about memory and identity, one that is also an exemplary entry in 20th-century Gothic fiction.

Stieg Larsson’s “Millennium Trilogy” is spectacular as a whole, but The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo stands out for several reasons. The book introduces us to journalist Mikael Blomkvist, who is facing jail time after losing a libel case. Although Blomkvist retreats from the public eye, he takes an interest in a curious disappearance case after meeting Henrik Vanger, the CEO of Vanger Enterprises. Blomkvist, however, isn’t the only person involved, as the exceptionally gifted investigator Lisbeth Salander has been hired to evaluate his history and skill set. The novel is a labyrinth of clues, red herrings, and twists, along with a gritty exploration of abuse and institutional failure.

According to recent reports, if you like the Oscar-winning neo-noir mystery, Mystic River, chances are that you’ll also like the book it is based on. Three boys — Dave, Sean, and Jimmy — grow up together in Boston. Tragedy strikes when Dave is abducted, and he returns after managing to escape, deeply traumatized. Fast-forward 25 years; the three men have been shaped by their respective circumstances, brought together by a grisly murder and the unsavory realization that one of them might be involved. Mystic River is a book that delves beneath the surface, compelling us to understand how grief carries on into adulthood. There’s immense thematic weight to this book about the tussle between choice and fatalism in the face of injustice.

  • According to recent reports, duty and Honor is the upcoming expansion for the critically acclaimed deck-building game, Star Trek: Captain's Chair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Star Trek fans will almost certainly be familiar with the legendary character Worf. The Klingon, first introduced in Star Trek: The Next Generation, has appeared in more episodes throughout the entire show's history than any other character, making him both a fan-favorite staple and a constant fixture. It is for this very reason that his reappearance on multiple reveals and subsequent fresh Star Trek content no longer feels terribly surprising, although it is always appreciated.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, for those who cannot get enough of Worf and want a brand-latest Star Trek release to tide them over, the iconic character is returning once more in a new release that is targeted at dedicated fans. Titled Duty and Honor, this new Star Trek project offers a different type of experience than the one most fans will be used to, all while putting Worf front and center. Suffice it to say, it could end up being the definitive Worf Star Trek release should its creators play their cards right.

According to recent reports, duty and Honor is the upcoming expansion for the critically acclaimed deck-building game, Star Trek: Captain's Chair. The base game, for those who've missed out thus far, is an in-depth, strategic experience in which players take on the role of one of six captains (either Picard, Sisko, Burnham, Shran, Koloth, and Sela) and must attempt to complete various objectives and obtain the highest score by playing cards from each character's corresponding starter deck and any they obtain throughout.

Recent findings suggest that widely praised as being a compelling and highly detailed Star Trek experience with strong theming and phenomenal representation of the characters included, Captain's Chair (developed by WizKids) has gone on to get multiple expansions. The latest, the aforementioned Duty and Honor, adds four new captains to the experience, as well as their corresponding decks, thus greatly increasing the level of replayability and variety within the game.

Duty and Honor is adding Captain Worf as well as the fan-favorite Deep Space Nine Cardassian, Gul Dukat. Two additional captains will also be added, although WizKids has not yet confirmed who they will be. Of course, included in their decks will be iconic ships, characters, and locations associated with them, so dedicated fans are in for a treat. While it isn't quite a newly introduced series, it should hopefully make up for the canceled Worf series that fans never got the chance to see.

The base Star Trek: Captain's Chair game that is required to play the Duty and Honor expansion costs $59.99. It is currently available for back-order on the official WizKids website and is expected to be shipped in Q4 2026.

The Duty and Honor expansion for Star Trek: Captain's Chair costs $39.99. It is currently available for pre-order via the official WizKids website, as well as other assorted retailers. It is estimated to have a release date of Q3 2027, according to the official store listing, which means it'll release any time between July 1 and September 30. Considering how well-received the other Star Trek: Captain's Chair expansions have been, fans can likely rest assured that Duty and Honor will do Worf proud.

Industry observers note that prime Video has been serving up a feast for romantic comedy fans in 2026. Lili Reinhart's rom-com "The Love Hypothesis" just finished dominating the Prime Video charts, which came in the wake of Ester Expósito's romantic thriller "Drawn Together" becoming a Prime streaming hit. Now, the streamer has added a Christmas-themed romance just in time for the holidays, and this one stars "Landman" actor Michelle Randolph.

Recent findings suggest that the film is called "Clashing Through the Snow" and before you immediately close this window just let me explain. Yes, the name sounds like the result of a "give me a cheesy Christmas rom-com title" ChatGPT prompt, but Randolph alone should pique your interest. The actor has quietly been delivering standout performances in Taylor Sheridan's "Landman" and his "Yellowstone" prequel "1923." The former sees her play Ainsley Norris, the ditzy but determined daughter of Billy Bob Thornton's oil man Tommy Norris. Based on her performances in those highlights, Randolph surely has a bright future ahead. While "Clashing Through the Snow" might not be her major breakthrough, it's doing pretty darn well on Prime Video.

Until recently, Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale's sports movie "Madden" was topping the Prime Video charts. But it's now been knocked out of the top spot by this festive romance movie, in which publishing editor Hannah Hendricks (Randolph) is forced to take a road trip with her rival, Ryan Mitchell (Chris Briney). You can see where this is going.

According to streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, the film has now hit number two on the United States overall Prime Video chart (which combines TV and films) as of Thanksgiving day, and sits at number one on the movie chart. But Michelle Randolph's comedy is proving popular elsewhere, too. In fact, it's become a global hit. At the time of writing, the film is charting on 61 countries' top 10 movie rankings, which is a pretty good showing. Even more impressive, "Clashing Through the Snow" is number one on the movie charts in 47 of those countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the movie has managed to break into the overall chart in 30 countries, taking the top spot in five of them. That means "Clashing Through the Snow" is the most-watched piece of media on Prime Video in Austria, Poland, Portugal, South Africa, and Switzerland. It even managed to hit number one on the overall chart in the U.S. on November 25, 2026. That's a notable achievement, as often films will break into the top 10 movies without making it onto the overall charts. "Clashing Through the Snow" must be good, then...

According to recent reports, "Clashing Through the Snow" is a comfortingly familiar rom-com outing that's perfect for the holidays. The film sees Chris Briney's Ryan Mitchell and Michelle Randolph's Hannah Hendricks stranded at an airport during a snowstorm, after which they share a rental car and set out on a cross-country trip to New York. The pair both need to close a deal in order to save their jobs — but wouldn't you know it, they fall in love instead. Along the way there's plenty of romantic Christmas movie moments as the couple stop in charming small towns and overcome mishaps together. Is "Clashing Through the Snow" pushing the boundaries of rom-coms? No. Is it charming? Sure is.

The film is directed by Carlson Young, who made her feature directorial debut with the 2021 fantasy horror "The Blazing World" before directing Sophie Turner in 2025's "Trust." She also oversaw a couple of Prime Video rom-coms before "Clashing Through the Snow," directing 2024's "Upgraded" and 2026's "The Last Sunrise.".

Now, she's delivered a major hit with her Randolph-led Christmas rom-com, which has a 77% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. There aren't enough reviews to earn it a critic score yet, but while William Bibbiani of TheWrap found it to be "unapologetically clichéd" he also found the dialogue to be memorable and saw the film as "an efficient delivery mechanism for semi-believable rom and semi-funny com.".

If that sounds appealing, "Clashing Through the Snow" is streaming on Prime Video right now.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing.
