In a recent development, amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the issue is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:.

In a recent development, in the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours! Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season.

According to recent reports, but before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

It has been revealed that no need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so quickly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the major drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

Industry observers note that then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves promptly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other reveals tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

The opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

The latter goal is harder and, arguably, more crucial. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) demonstrates up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

It has been revealed that there’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” concern, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

Outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

In a recent development, how Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of big, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

So long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover new sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

#142964. How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every visual element in animation helps tell the story.
  • According to recent reports, and by “more,” we mean witches.
  • “Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something newly introduced inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

According to recent reports, and by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

“Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

It has been revealed that according to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”.

Recent findings suggest that but the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

Sources indicate that “The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”.

Recent findings suggest that billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn said. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”.

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”.

It has been revealed that one key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”.

According to recent reports, but Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie noted yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”.

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”.

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”.

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush noted.

“Hexed” is now playing in theaters.

Sources indicate that the Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same firm, Reto, that introduced a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too. Eight of the styles have a one-in-eight chance of finding, while the ninth style is only found in one out of every 64 boxes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to modern thriller book series, Lee Child is an author readers trust more than many others. His rapid-fire rhythmic storytelling, explosive narrative arcs, and heroes with an unwavering sense of justice have captivated fans for decades. His multi-award-winning Jack Reacher novels have come to define the genre in the present day, with Child’s tale of a wandering former military policeman being a literary thriller staple since Reacher made his debut in 1997’s The Killing Floor.

Recent findings suggest that the only problem with the Reacher books is deciding what to read afterward. They’re almost too good. Plenty of thrillers offer violence and conspiracies, but fewer deliver that same combination of gripping action and a protagonist who makes losing oneself in thousands of pages across an entire series feel like light work. Fortunately, Mark Greaney’s The Gray Man novels offer both, and they have an endorsement from Lee Child himself to prove it. For Reacher fans who’ve devoured everything from The Killing Floor to 2026’s Chain Reaction, Greaney’s The Gray Man saga is the perfect next step, especially with a January release giving readers another reason to discover the series’ lethal yet surprisingly principled leading man.

Rather than a military cop turned drifter, The Gray Man books follow Court Gentry, a former CIA operative turned assassin whose extraordinary abilities repeatedly collide with his stubborn moral code. There are 15 published novels so far, starting with 2009’s The Gray Man, providing plenty of dangerous assignments and double-crosses that are bound to delight any Reacher fan. The latest, The Hard Line, reaches US paperback on January 12, 2027. That makes the newest installment in this Barry Award-winning series easier than ever to dive into for Reacher readers seeking a latest literary character to obsess over.

Sources indicate that mark Greaney’s The Gray Man novels have attracted plenty of impressive endorsements, but one particularly persuasive recommendation keeps appearing in press releases, blurbs, and book covers: Lee Child’s declaration, “I love the Gray Man.” It’s a short statement with considerable weight. Few authors understand the appeal of a resourceful, dangerous thriller novel protagonist better than Lee Child, and his approval immediately gives Reacher readers a reason to dive into Greaney’s world.

Sources indicate that for any fans of Jack Reacher, the explosive sequence of events that unfold once Court Gentry’s enemies start underestimating him are bound to resonate. Both series understand the satisfaction of watching an exceptionally capable outsider dismantle an opponent’s carefully constructed plan. Money, manpower, and official authority offer little protection against characters like Reacher and Gentry, both of whom can identify a weakness and exploit it before anyone realizes what’s happening. Crucially, the intelligence of both heroes matters as much as their capacity for violence. Just like the best Reacher novels, the thrill and joy of The Gray Man books is in seeing how Gentry assesses a seemingly impossible situation, then discovering just how badly their adversaries have misjudged them.

It has been revealed that there’s also a moral stubbornness beneath the brutality that makes The Gray Man’s Gentry a character fans of Lee Child’s Jack Reacher are all-but-guaranteed to fall in love with. Gentry’s profession makes him complicated, but his personal code gives readers something solid to hold onto amid shifting loyalties. Like Reacher, he’s endearing because doing the right thing can make his life considerably harder, but that never leads him to compromise his moral values. That tension keeps the momentum high and the action emotionally grounded. Gentry is, just like Reacher, a character readers want him to survive, and it’s because his commitment to doing the right thing makes him someone worth supporting.

Recent findings suggest that however, nobody should be mistaken into thinking that The Gray Man has nothing to distinguish itself. Mark Greaney gives the familiar appeal of the Jack Reacher novels a distinctive espionage setting that sets his own series and characters apart. Where Reacher frequently uncovers trouble in American communities, Gentry operates amid international intelligence networks, covert missions, and betrayals with consequences across borders. Greaney’s extensive research and training with military and law enforcement personnel help give those encounters a substantial level of detail and authenticity. The result is a book series that offers Reacher fans familiar pleasures while opening up a much larger, more treacherous world.

You can purchase The Gray Man, the first book in the series, here.

The run-up January next year is a great time for Reacher fans to start exploring Court Gentry’s world, especially if paperbacks are their go-to format. The Hard Line, the fifteenth and latest The Gray Man novel, arrived in hardcover and ebook through Berkley on February 17, 2026, alongside its audiobook edition. Its US paperback follows on January 12, 2027, nearly eleven months later. For readers who prefer paperbacks, that wait brings a chance to experience one of the best The Gray Man novels without having to carry around a clunky hardback, but with something more physical than an ebook.

Recent findings suggest that the Hard Line has been celebrated by existing fans of The Gray Man because of how deeply personal the latest conspiracy Gentry gets swept up in becomes. Intelligence personnel are being targeted, while Mark Greaney’s globe-trotting hero faces an assassin whose revenge threatens the people he cares about, including his estranged father. The family dynamic gives the danger an emotional force beyond another hazardous white-knuckle assignment.

Gentry’s extraordinary competence can, of course, keep him alive, but protecting everyone around him is a much less certain proposition. The book has been praised for making an established action hero feel vulnerable again. There aren’t really any bad books in The Gray Man series, but The Hard Line’s combination of superb character development and escalating danger has ensured the series’ most recent installment was instantly celebrated as one of its best.

For Reacher readers who like the sound of a spectacle-heavy thriller that doesn’t skimp on serious consequences for its protagonist, January’s rerelease of The Hard Line is bringing considerably more than another collection of gunfights to paperback for the first time.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • While the late Anton Yelchin had found major success in movies like Green Room or even the modern Star Trek films, Cooke and Taylor-Joy were just getting started, some years away from the blockbuster extravaganzas of Dune and House of the Dragon.
  • Recent findings suggest that thoroughbreds is a movie of interiors, specializing in the rich, old money homes of its protagonists Amanda (Olivia Cooke) and Lily (Anya Taylor-Joy), who live in suburban Connecticut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of the most unsung releases of the last decade was 2017’s Thoroughbreds, a thriller deep in the film noir mode with three great actors going toe to toe. With Anya Taylor-Joy, Olivia Cooke, and Anton Yelchin as the architects and participants of a murder plot, it’s less a crime movie and more of a character study, with director Cory Finley mining both pathos and extremely dark comedy from the premise. In an era where minimal-location movies about the sociopathy of the rich were frequently successful discourse machines (including Taylor-Joy’s 2022 vehicle The Menu), Thoroughbreds was a classically amoral story of kids whose wealth insulates them from consequences, yet you still root for them. The movie was unfortunately ahead of the curve with its note-perfect plotting and criminal ideation, as well as its cast.

While the late Anton Yelchin had found major success in movies like Green Room or even the modern Star Trek films, Cooke and Taylor-Joy were just getting started, some years away from the blockbuster extravaganzas of Dune and House of the Dragon. Coming some years before that, Thoroughbreds suggested great depth from all three actors, playing them against each other as they all fight for their own agendas, while also giving viewers the chance to identify with potentially evil teens. The movie is leaving Starz on November 30, but its study of youthful sociopathy and the tenuous nature of female friendship means it should remain a cult classic for years to come.

Recent findings suggest that thoroughbreds is a movie of interiors, specializing in the rich, old money homes of its protagonists Amanda (Olivia Cooke) and Lily (Anya Taylor-Joy), who live in suburban Connecticut. From the very beginning, when Amanda mercy-kills her crippled horse (leading to the title) in an unnerving moment, the movie keeps its distance from the characters, with director Cory Finley’s camera holding on scenes and moments for long stretches. Rather than the aspirational gleeful immorality of the classic teenage murderer movie Heathers, Thoroughbreds is methodical and ironic. The fancy decor, the emotional repression, and the basement tanning beds all go hand in hand with Amanda’s claims of an inability to feel anything. You might wonder if she’s just being an edgy teenager, especially after the horse euthanizing moment. But the movie’s visual language backs her up.

It has been revealed that in a twist directly out of Alfred Hitchcock’s Strangers on a Train, the movie’s narrative begins to hinge on a murderous favor. Lily, effectively tasked by Amanda’s mom to befriend her troubled daughter, has an abusive stepfather named Mark (Paul Sparks), and Amanda, in her emotionless wisdom, presents a solution: kill him. The girls have a means of laundering the murder in the form of drug dealer Tim (Yelchin). Olivia Cooke’s portrayal of Amanda veers beyond creating an empathetic version of somebody suffering from an undisclosed mental illness, but it never goes into villain territory either. The movie’s cold and heavily adorned visual sensibility might have Yorgos Lanthimos-esque ironic distance from what you see, but it means that the relationship between the two girls becomes increasingly complex, in a way that it wouldn’t be if viewers were directly keyed into how the girls see each other.

Industry observers note that cory Finley had reportedly envisioned the movie as a play originally, and that feeling lingers in the film. The minimal cast and locations, as well as the long takes and reliance on dialogue, have the potential to feel theatrical, but the movie is sophisticated on the level of cinematic storytelling, commenting on its cast with its staging and using its widescreen compositions for both comedy and terror as chickens come home to roost. As he told IndieWire, the story began with the idea of a character who couldn’t feel anything. As the friend seeking to take advantage of that to help her own family situation, Anya Taylor-Joy’s Lily is effectively not much different.

The movie’s cinematic lineage is rich, drawing from Alfred Hitchcock (besides Strangers on a Train, his highly theatrical one-take experiment Rope, with its homoerotic murder conspiracy, has a clear line to Thoroughbreds) as well as ‘90s evil rich kid movies like Cruel Intentions, but with a much less moral stance. Peter Jackson’s true-crime classic Heavenly Creatures also feels like an influence, with the fantastical sequences substituted for cold stylization. When Amanda and Lily’s prepares go awry, we see the truth of what the girls are willing to go through with, how calculating they can be with the other’s emotional headspace. A different movie about teenage murder conspirators might let them off the hook, but Amanda’s dreams of wild thoroughbred horses suggest that a cruel end is coming to everybody.

It has been revealed that openAI is bringing GPT-6.2 Sol to the Chat tab in ChatGPT today, less than a week after the model debuted in Work and Codex. The company also set a retirement date for two older models.

OpenAI states it tuned this version of Sol for everyday conversation. It’s better at picking out details in photos, like the symbols on a parking sign, and following your instructions when searching the web.

In a recent development, if you’re comparing hotels for a weekend trip, for example, ChatGPT can weigh a shorter walk against a lower nightly rate. It can also offer to alert you when something you’re shopping for drops in price.

The global rollout starts today for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise people.

As for the outgoing models, OpenAI states it will retire GPT-5.6 Sol from Chat, Work, and Codex on December 23.

GPT-5.6 Terra will also leave ChatGPT Work and Codex on the same day next month.

To get these latest features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the problem with its fresh Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:.

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground.

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Customers won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while Harlan Coben had penned a handful of Myron Bolitar novels before writing the book that Netflix adapted into a show in 2021, the series was based on one of his first standalone novels. If Prime Video’s Reacher franchise proves one thing, it is that streaming fans love a good page-to-screen adaptation. To be more specific, streaming show adaptations of best-selling crime, thriller, and mystery novels tend to fare extraordinarily well on Prime Video, Netflix, Hulu, and Peacock alike.

Recent findings suggest that whether it is an adaptation of Andrea Mara’s novel All Her Fault breaking viewing records on Peacock or Netflix’s 30-episode take on Matthew Quick’s book The Night Agent rivaling Reacher in its popularity, the formula has proven a hit over and over again. Recently, Prime Video’s Cross cashed in on this trend, although the streaming service’s 2014 hit Bosch and its many spinoffs pioneered the approach over a decade earlier.

Recent findings suggest that however, the legendary crime writer Harlan Coben is something of an unusual case when it comes to streaming indicates. Coben first became a bestselling author back in 1990 with his standalone novel Play Dead, followed, by 1991’s Miracle Cure. However, it was the 12-book Myron Bolitar series that made Coben a star, beginning with 1995’s Deal Breaker. Despite the popularity of this novel series, Netflix has mostly adapted his standalone books, like Gone for Good, to the screen rather than Myron Bolitar novels.

Related in 2002, Gone for Good was a major hit for Coben. The novel follows Will, who is horrified to learn the disturbing truth about his brother Ken’s disappearance eleven years earlier after his girlfriend goes missing in the present day. Released in August 2021, Gone for Good’s Netflix adaptation relocated the story to France and changed some names accordingly, starring Finnegan Oldfield as Guillaume and Nicolas Duvauchelle as his missing brother, Fred.

It has been revealed that unlike Prime Video’s Reacher franchise, Netflix’s Coben adaptations all feature different main characters in stories that have no canon connections. Even though there are plenty of Myron Bolitar books to adapt, and many more YA spinoff novels starring his nephew Mickey, the streaming service has thus far opted to focus instead on Coben’s standalone efforts. These include No Second Chance, The Stranger, The Innocent, The Woods, Gone For Good, Stay Close, Hold Tight, Fool Me Once, Missing You, Run Away, and I Will Always Find You.

If that list seems long, that’s because it is. All told, there are 13 Coben demonstrates on Netflix, with seven being English-language productions, while a further six are foreign-language shows like Gone For Good. Interestingly enough, much like Michael Connelly’s The Lincoln Lawyer was a Matthew McConaughey movie before the novel series became a Netflix show, the first screen adaptation of Coben’s work was a feature length movie, director Guillame Canet’s 2006 thriller Tell No One.

If the fact that Tell No One and Gone For Good are French-language productions didn’t give it away, Coben’s work has a massive worldwide fan base that spans the globe. His twisty thrillers translate well into other languages, which is why The Woods, Just One Look, and Hold Tight were Polish productions, The Innocent is a Spanish series, and 2025’s Caught hailed from Argentina.

It has been revealed that between that Coben series and the same year’s long-awaited comic adaptation The Eternaut, Argentina is emerging as a major hub for Netflix highlights. However, it is tough to beat some of the writer’s earliest shows. With its clever twists, inventive plotting, and poignant character work, Netflix’s 2021 hit Gone For Good remains one of the author’s most underrated adaptations to date.

While these recent examples have earned considerable attention, and rightfully so, they are not the first. In fact, Snowpiercer took a similar approach in 2020. The series creates an immersive world full of danger and division that all fans of the genre should watch.

Sources indicate that snowpiercer delivers a unique premise and incredible worldbuilding that sets it apart. Inspired by the 2013 film of the same name, the story isn't totally original, but the series builds on the concept that always deserved more than two hours. And Snowpiercer certainly expands the idea with four unforgettable seasons. Though it may not have gained the popularity that other comparable series have, it still deserves attention. Six years later, Snowpiercer is the perfect binge watch for anyone who loves sci-fi thrillers, dystopian worlds, or complex moral questions.

It has been revealed that snowpiercer features a world like no other, where a massive luxury train is the only place people can live. Eerily set in 2026, the story takes place seven years after an environmental disaster created a upcoming ice age, killing much of human civilization. However, some survive on a constantly moving train designed by eccentric billionaire Mr. Joseph Wilford (Sean Bean). While the movement keeps them alive, the survivors continue to struggle. The system is strictly divided into distinct social classes. The elite live in the front, third-class laborers keep the machine running, and the stowaways, known as the Tailies, are just trying to survive. However, the dynamic alters when a series of murders threatens the train. Head Engineer Melanie Cavill (Jennifer Connelly) pulls Chicago police officer Andre Layton (Daveed Diggs) up from the Tail to uncover the truth.

According to recent reports, layton has his own motivations. He dreams of revolution and believes this investigation can take him one step closer, allowing him to map out the train. However, the fallout spirals as the train is full of secrets. Most prominently, the passengers begin to realize that inventor Joseph Wilford isn't running the train because Melanie abandoned him during boarding, leaving him for dead. Although this society is confined to a train, Snowpiercer covers a lot of ground as it explores the brutal realities of civilization, oppression, and unavoidable moral questions of survival. This is the crux of the series, giving it a dark and fascinating tone.

What stands out most about Snowpiercer is its worldbuilding. A train is an uncharacteristic setting, but it comes with plenty to explore as the series delves into how different biomes separate the classes, how food is grown, and even how the passengers deal with their dead. These may seem like small details, but they reveal a lot about the world and the desperate characters who inhabit it. Through these elements, the series brings this society to life and creates something upcoming. As the story goes on, Snowpiercer even explores beyond the train, showing the devastation of the icy world and further immersing the audience in the dystopian setting.

According to recent reports, though this concept is rare, the story is inspired by the movie, but the two are far from the same. Of course, there are similarities, but Snowpiercer isn't even strictly a remake. The series takes the concept, but uses different characters and circumstances to tell its own story. With significantly more time, the series sets a slower pace, building tension and introducing the world a little at a time, which is a luxury the film doesn't have. Ultimately, that dedication to the story is what makes Snowpiercer work. The series stands out, even as the dystopian genre grows, and though it's a few years old now, Snowpiercer is an unmatched sci-fi watch that deserves more attention.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to massive issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

In a recent development, andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he notes he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

According to recent reports, ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he notes can yield “small data” solutions to major issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

Recent findings suggest that the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Industry observers note that andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having mentioned that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

According to recent reports, ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

In a recent development, having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of owners, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of customers.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from significant data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

Industry observers note that I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and remarked, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing newly introduced here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and noted, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

It has been revealed that the data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one organization or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For significant data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

It has been revealed that for example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very promptly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Latest tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an key piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is crucial, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention swiftly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

In a recent development, ng: I think synthetic data is an crucial tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion consumers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Industry observers note that synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these problems more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a firm approaches Landing AI and indicates it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Sources indicate that ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

Recent findings suggest that how do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift concern. I find it really notable to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and patch the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

Recent findings suggest that in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion owners. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

In a recent development, ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent fresh neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s key for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print glitch as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

After Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov becomes the first person to walk on the Moon and defeats NASA's Apollo 11 mission, the entire geopolitical landscape shifts greatly, forcing the United States into a compromising position as they look to regain their presence in outer space.

It has been revealed that losing the Space Race actually accelerates the American space program, which launches an epic sci-fi saga that serves as the foundation of For All Mankind. Rather than setting the fresh global standard for space missions, the U.S. follows the lead of the Soviets, which includes recruiting more female astronauts and building permanent infrastructure on the moon. The series explores how these alternate historical events reshape American politics and culture, even down to the fabric of everyday life, which creates a fascinating viewing experience.

What's more, For All Mankind goes even further than Moon operations in its later seasons and eventually expands to Mars, adding another compelling angle to the epic space sci-fi saga. Essentially, losing the initial Space Race catapults technological advancement in the United States' space program, so much so that the Space Race never actually ends. By the time season 5 arrives, a large colony has been firmly established on Mars in the year 2012, sparking interplanetary conflict as seen in other exceptional sci-fi masterpieces like The Expanse.

Determined to recover from losing the race to the Moon, the United States shifts its gears to rapidly inhabit Mars, which only thickens the plot and raises the stakes in the series.

The sixth and final season of For All Mankind will jump into the 2020s and chronicle the growing situation on Mars, following the first human ever born off Earth. Because Apple TV has confirmed that For All Mankind will be the last, viewers can expect a conclusive ending to the decades-long space race portrayed in the series, likely bringing the series to even fresh heights in terms of stakes and tension. Several of the miniseries that HBO has produced over the last couple of decades are not just another feather in their hat but icons of their genre, TV classics of their time, and standouts among their contemporaries.

Industry observers note that while 2001’s Band of Brothers has become the gold standard for war-drama television, 2019’s Chernobyl excels in translating a traumatic human event into an intricate character study. Between adaptations of bestselling novels and intriguing original stories, here are our picks for elite HBO miniseries that you can binge right now.

Scottish comedian and actor Richard Gadd of Baby Reindeer fame returns with another chilling miniseries, Half Man, which he also writes and stars in. The six-part psychological thriller unspools the complicated, violent, lifelong friendship between Gadd’s Ruben and Jamie Bell’s Niall, after an unexpected incident at Niall’s wedding forces them to reconnect with their past. Stuart Campbell and Mitchell Robertson portray the younger versions of Ruben and Niall.

Industry observers note that half Man is a story about toxic male friendships, but it is the show’s treatment that makes it more intense and raw than most. While Niall is an intricately written character, Ruben is a drastic departure from Gadd’s fragile, sensitive role in Baby Reindeer, and the actor-comedian thrives as the aggressive, tormented character. Deeply disturbing yet delicate in its own way, Half Man is an exceptionally intense show that easily ranks among the best TV dramas made in the 2020s.

Industry observers note that created by Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks in their second collaboration following Saving Private Ryan, Band of Brothers is a 21st-century television classic adapted from the non-fiction book by Stephen E. Ambrose. Set during WWII, the war drama recounts the story of the “Easy” Company, 2nd Battalion, 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment of the 101st Airborne Division of the US Army on the Western Front between D-Day and their occupation of Berchtesgaden. Kirk Acevedo, Eion Bailey, Damian Lewis, Ron Livingston, and Neal McDonough portray various real-life characters.

Band of Brothers became an instant classic when it premiered 25 years ago and has since been an HBO landmark and often cited as a benchmark of the genre. The 10-episode miniseries combines a dramatized narrative with documentary-style, candid interviews with real veterans, reconstructing one of the grimmest times of human history in the most thoughtful way. A remarkable tribute to the sacrifices of a whole generation of American soldiers, Band of Brothers is surely a must-watch for genre fans.

Created by David Simon, Ed Burns, and Evan Wright, Generation Kill is an often-forgotten war miniseries that adapts Wright’s non-fiction book of the same name, chronicling his experiences as an embedded reporter in the US Marine Corps during the 2003 Invasion of Iraq. Set during the first phase of the war, the series follows Wright, played by Lee Tergesen, as he rides along with the U.S. Marine Corps' 1st Reconnaissance Battalion on their way to Baghdad. Other real-life people are portrayed by Alexander Skarsgård, Billy Rush, James Ransone, and Stark Sands.

Generation Kill is often considered one of the most visceral and grounded portrayals of war on television. At the time of its broadcast, it was among the most prestigious indicates of the genre and is undeniably one of the best war shows of the 2000s. However, despite its critical acclaim and several accolades, Generation Kill has mostly faded from mainstream attention and has been overshadowed by bigger productions.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

It has been revealed that you want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

Industry observers note that you go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

It has been revealed that you say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

Created by David E. Kelley, The Undoing is loosely based on Jean Hanff Korelitz’s novel You Should Have Known and follows Grace (Nicole Kidman), a wealthy therapist in Upcoming York City, whose perfect life begins to unravel when her renowned oncologist husband, Dr. Jonathan Fraser (Hugh Grant), is accused of murder. As the investigation proceeds, Grace and her family learn shocking truths about Jonathan, making her question her marriage, profession, and the truth of her life. Other key cast members include Noma Dumezweni, Édgar Ramírez, Donald Sutherland, and Noah Jupe.

According to recent reports, elevated by the star power of its cast and refined production design, The Undoing is truly an elite miniseries and one of the finest HBO has produced in the 2020s. Nicole Kidman and Hugh Grant steal every scene with their commanding presence, even if the plot loses momentum occasionally, making this six-episode psychological crime thriller a highly engaging watch. The show has earned praise for its acting, cinematography, and strong plot twists, but has also been criticized for its writing and pacing.

Now considered one of the most immersive screen portrayals of the disaster of 1986, Chernobyl is a dramatized retelling of the titular nuclear plant explosion in Ukraine that resulted in the devastation of all life in the region for decades. The series takes a closer look at the accident from the perspectives of all the key people involved, exploring the events leading up to it and its aftermath. The show boasts a strong ensemble cast, with Jared Harris, Stellan Skarsgård, Emily Watson, Paul Ritter, Jessie Buckley, and more in notable roles.

Sources indicate that created by Craig Mazin, Chernobyl is a masterfully made miniseries that cleverly unpacks the horrific history within its limited runtime. While the show takes some dramatic liberties, trading fact for fiction, it does so engagingly, with powerful performances and an atmospheric setting. The series has since remained a critical darling and a fan favorite, distinctly capturing the emotional and physical intensity of the real tragedy.

Starring Kate Winslet as protagonist Marianne “Mare” Sheehan, Mare of Easttown follows the titular police detective in a small Philadelphia town, where she attempts to solve the murder of a local teenager while being tormented by a similar case from a year ago. Mare continues to search for truth while grappling with past guilt, the loss of a child, divorce, and her declining reputation. Julianne Nicholson, Jean Smart, Angourie Rice, and Guy Pearce also star in key roles.

According to recent reports, when Mare of Easttown first premiered, it was a class of its own as a crime drama thriller miniseries. Its gritty story, grounded characters, and deeply emotional plotlines all come together to make this an intense show that is sure to leave an impact on the audience long after the credits roll. Created by Brad Ingelsby, Mare of Easttown has become a modern classic for HBO that thrives on Kate Winslet’s exceptional, award-winning performance, which is often considered her TV best.

According to recent reports, based on Criminal Justice by Peter Moffat and created by Richard Price and Steven Zaillian, The Night Of centers on a Pakistani-American college student named Nasir “Naz” Khan (Riz Ahmed), who wakes up after a nightlong party fueled by drugs and alcohol next to the dead body of a woman he met the night before. With missing memories of the night and evidence pointing to him as the killer, Naz leaves his fate in the hands of a resolute lawyer named John Stone (John Turturro). Bill Camp, Michael Kenneth Williams, and Poorna Jagannathan appear in key roles.

Recent findings suggest that the Night Of is an excellently made crime drama that grips the audience with its tightly-knit plot and deep, character-driven storytelling. The show’s creators elevate the original material by putting an intelligent spin on classic tropes and making it a timely story. When it premiered, the crime thriller was critically praised for its masterful production, layered characterizations, and riveting performances by Turturro and Ahmed.

A Southern Gothic psychological thriller miniseries created by Marti Noxon, Sharp Objects is a series adaptation of Gillian Flynn’s debut novel of the same name and follows Camille Preaker (Amy Adams), a reporter suffering from alcoholism and psychological troubles, who returns to her hometown in Missouri. Recently discharged from a psychiatric hospital and returning to her controlling mother, Adora (Patricia Clarkson), Camille is forced to confront her personal demons while investigating the murder of two young girls. Chris Messina and Eliza Scanlen also have main roles.

In a recent development, the HBO adaptation of Sharp Objects stays true to Flynn’s original crime novel in tone and themes but varies in format and pacing. In fact, the slow-burn storytelling balances the show’s atmospheric setting and dark themes to better explore the characters’ fractured psyches and meditate on their emotional states. Headlined by intense performances from Adams and Clarkson, Sharp Objects is one of HBO's best crime thriller miniseries of the 2010s.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler states that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

Recent findings suggest that I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

Sources indicate that the “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler says, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

Industry observers note that there’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting tech giant to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

Industry observers note that the best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

It has been revealed that advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in September, Apple held a photography exhibition in Newly introduced York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

According to recent reports, the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition).

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

Sources indicate that “The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”.

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in New York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

It has been revealed that the exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that rather than attempting to match Pratchett's renown on his own turf, Discworld has instead pivoted to a different medium, with a number of recent products focusing on the tabletop market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the years since Terry Pratchett's death, fans of his Discworld have had to come to terms with the end of the series, as it's hard to imagine anyone else being able to take up the mantle and spin up newly introduced books that deliver an equal level of cleverness. Recently, though, the wheels of the Discworld franchise have started to spin once more, and it's clear that a large portion of the community is on board.

It has been revealed that rather than attempting to match Pratchett's renown on his own turf, Discworld has instead pivoted to a different medium, with a number of recent products focusing on the tabletop market. The latest, Terry Pratchett's Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, took only 30 minutes to prove itself as an immediate smash hit.

Terry Pratchett's Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald went live on November 3 on the crowdfunding platform Gamefound, and according to the platform's statistics, it reached its£50,000 funding goal in 30 minutes and 32 seconds. In the weeks since, it's managed to leave that original goal in the dust, raising a total of £678,861.96 from 3,660 backers, or 1,357.72% of the goal. For reference, that's the rough equivalent of $890,000 USD, against an original goal of roughly $65,500.

Sources indicate that the new book provides a rulebook for tabletop roleplaying in Lancre and Überwald, two neighboring regionslocated to the north and northeast of Ankh-Morpork. Lancre draws inspiration from rural England, particularly in the northern part of the country, while Überwald is essentially Discworld's version of Transylvania. Along with details on the setting and lore,Adventures in Lancre and Überwaldadds appropriate playable races and magic options, letting players take on the roles of vampires, werewolves, and witches.

Recent findings suggest that terry Pratchett's Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald follows up on Terry Pratchett's Discworld: Adventures in Ankh-Morpork, which focused on the city-state at the heart of many of Pratchett's stories. The initial RPG product also proved to be a success overall, but its Kickstarter campaign had some challenges, which publisher Modiphius addresses in the first Gamefound post for the latest campaign. Modiphius is promising new EU distributors to speed up affairs in the region, increased communication, additional quality control, clearer product descriptions, and an extra emphasis on safe shipping and packaging.

According to recent reports, when contrasted with a typical TTRPG product like D&D, the Discworld RPG places a greater emphasis on open-ended traits rather than determining player abilities primarily through stats. At the game table, this means that arguing with the game master is encouraged, at least in the sense of stating cases and twisting words as to why your character should be able to succeed at something. It's also much more focused on story than combat, which could make it fun for those who are drawn to Discworld because of the writing (read: everyone).

Opinions on just how successful the design concepts of the Discworld RPG are have been varied, but there's clearly enough excitement around the product to fuel this very successful follow-up. Hopefully, Terry Pratchett's Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwaldcan lean into everything that works and expand or improve on anything that didn't.

The iPhone 17e was rolled out in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.
